description: Shared Docker building blocks for TestFramework container environments: declaring where an application comes from and building it, network creation, host and network endpoint addressing, readiness waits and container log capture.
releaseNotes:
Building an image from a project no longer depends on the registry being reachable.
Changed in 0.1.1:
- The .NET SDK fetches the base image's manifest from a registry on every image build, even when that exact image is already in the local daemon. Where that request fails - a broken IPv6 path is the common cause, and a PPPoE line behind a VPN is enough - the SDK spent about two and a half minutes retrying and then failed with CONTAINER1006, which named neither the cause nor a way out.
- That is now detected before the SDK is started, by asking the daemon whether the base image is here and the registry whether it answers. Both cost milliseconds. When the image is here and the registry is not answering, the application is published to a directory and the image is built from the local copy, which contacts no registry.
- The probe is a hint rather than a verdict, because the failure is intermittent: when it is wrong the SDK is still tried, and the same recovery runs after it fails.
- Whichever route is taken is stated in the run log, and a plan built the second way carries a fallback reason. The failure message, when nothing can be done, now names the base image, the pull that would fix the machine, and the ContainerSource.Image(...) escape that needs no administrator rights.
- An image the daemon cannot pull is now fetched by the test process instead. Where the IPv6 path to a registry is broken - the TLS handshake dies on the certificate chain because it exceeds the real path MTU, and the ICMPv6 message that would report it is filtered - the daemon fails every pull while everything else on the machine works. Configuring this process's HTTP client cannot help, because the daemon makes that connection. So on a transport failure the image is downloaded here over a connection pinned to IPv4, written as an archive and handed over with 'docker load'. Measured on such a machine: the daemon's pull fails outright, the same image arrives in four seconds. Anonymous registries only; Docker Hub needs a token exchange this does not perform, and says so.
- An image is built once per run rather than once per environment. Two environments describing the same project, configuration, framework and base image used to each run their own publish and image build and throw the result away at teardown, so a suite of a dozen chapters against one unchanged application paid for a dozen identical builds. Measured on the showroom's web lane: 25 minutes down to under 3. Runs stay isolated - an image is read only, and every container still gets its own writable layer, settings and data - and a teardown no longer removes an image later environments still share.
- The SDK publish is bounded by three minutes rather than ten when the base image is already in the local daemon, because a publish that stops making progress is then a short detour rather than a lost run. Without a local fallback it keeps the full budget, so a slow machine is not turned into a failed run.
- Every dotnet invocation is now bounded by a timeout and killed with its process tree, on cancellation as well as on expiry. It previously had none: an SDK container publish reaching a registry that neither answers nor refuses does not fail, it wedges - observed as publishes still alive after ninety minutes, each holding a hung docker child, and outliving the stopped test run that started them. A wedged publish is now a failed one, which means the recovery above can actually run, and a cancelled run no longer leaks processes.
Worth knowing up front:
- Where a container's application comes from is declared, not guessed: Image(...), Project(...) - resolved against the file that declares it - or Directory(...). Project facts come from MSBuild rather than from inspecting paths, a multi-targeted project is a hard error instead of a silent pick, and the whole resolved plan is logged before anything is built, so a failure can be read against what was going to happen.
- Published ports bind to 127.0.0.1, not to every interface. A test SQL Server or emulator is no longer reachable from the rest of the network while a suite runs. Set TESTFRAMEWORK_CONTAINER_HOST_IP when the Docker daemon is remote and the loopback default would make the port unreachable.
- Docker host detection runs before the first connection. Docker Desktop on Windows exposes the engine under more than one named pipe, and picking the wrong one produced a connection failure on a machine where Docker was working fine.
- Images and temporary build output this package creates are labelled and swept when they are more than a day old, because a killed test host leaves them behind and the container reaper does not cover them. Set TESTFRAMEWORK_CONTAINER_NO_SWEEP to disable.
- Docker CLI invocations are bounded by a timeout, so a wedged CLI fails teardown instead of hanging it forever.
